implementation_notes: Sequence.filter(_ isIncluded: (Element) throws -> Bool) rethrows -> [Element] takes the criterion as a closure and returns a new array; the standard library documents that sequence operations taking closures are normally eager - 'they use the closure immediately and return a new array' - whereas the lazy property gives permission to store the closure and the sequence in a LazyFilterSequence and defer computation with no buffering. The container-typed copy is an initialiser call: func filtered(_ keep: (Threat) -> Bool) -> Self { Self(systemID: systemID, threats: threats.filter(keep)) }. Closures are non-escaping by default, so a criterion used only for the call costs no allocation, and rethrows lets a predicate fail (a criterion that reads a file) without a Result wrapper. No Filterer protocol is needed; a stored criterion is just a named function type, @escaping if retained.
pitfalls: filter returns an Array, so a container that is generic over its collection type (Set, ContiguousArray, custom Collection) must convert explicitly and may silently change element ordering or uniqueness.

A lazy chain stores the closure and the base sequence: a criterion that captures self or a large resource keeps it alive, and a lazy chain cannot propagate throws the way the eager rethrows overload does.
Capturing mutable class state in a stored criterion makes results depend on when the filtered view is traversed, and a lazy sequence that is traversed twice re-runs the predicate.
Filtering a String (a Collection of Character) or a Dictionary returns an array of characters/keys, not the original type - easy to miss when the call site looks type-preserving.
